solution: Every lateral face is planar and convex, so the surface distance from an apex to a point U on its base boundary is just the straight 3-D distance r(U) = sqrt(h^2 + |c-U|^2) (c = base centre); equivalently the lateral surface is a cone, every geodesic out of the cone point is radial, and such a geodesic never crosses a lateral edge. Unfolding the single face containing U about its base edge e makes that distance planar: |A' - U| with A' = midpoint(e) - sqrt(h^2+(s/2)^2) * outward_normal(e), i.e. the apex rotated flat ACROSS the edge (the outward image m + slant*n gives identical distances, since it is the mirror of A' in line e and U lies on e, but the unfolded path then bounces off e instead of crossing it, which silently breaks every crossing test). The answer is min over U on base 1's boundary and V on base 2's boundary of r1(U) + |U-V| + r2(V), using the plain straight ground distance with no obstacle test: it lower-bounds any walk (take U = last point on base 1, V = first point after it on base 2), and since r is 1-Lipschitz in ground distance, a minimiser whose segment cuts a convex base can be slid to where the segment leaves that base without increasing the value, so the minimum is attained by a legal walk. Fixing one base edge of each pyramid leaves min over U in e1, V in e2 of |A'-U| + |U-V| + |V-B'|, a jointly convex objective (a sum of norms of affine maps) on a product of two segments; run it over all 16 edge pairs, each solved by nested ternary search or in closed form - straight |A'B'| when the segment meets e1 and then e2, otherwise a base corner pins one endpoint (where r equals the lateral edge sqrt(h^2+s^2/2)) and the other is the classic reflect-and-clamp point-segment-point minimisation. Total work is O(1) for the single test case.
statement_summary: Two right square pyramids stand on a plane, each described by one directed base edge with the solid to its left and by a height; their bases overlap in zero area. An ant travels only across the pyramids' lateral surfaces and the ground. The problem asks for the minimum distance it walks between the two apexes, within an absolute or relative error of one part in a million.
notes: Vocabulary gaps (the two most discriminating ideas have no canonical slug): (i) UNFOLDING / net-of-a-polyhedron - flattening a face about an edge so a surface geodesic becomes a straight planar segment, the whole content of this problem; (ii) GEODESIC / shortest path on a surface - 'shortest-path' is categorised 'graph' in the taxonomy and there is no graph here, so it is carried as a tag only, not as a pattern, to keep the query 'shortest path' reaching this problem without asserting Dijkstra/BFS. 'ternary-search' is kept at 0.6 rather than dropped: the convex two-segment minimisation is what most accepted solutions actually run (nested ternary), but it is a route, not a necessity - verify_carlsvacation.py check (b) shows an O(1) closed form agreeing with it to 1.8e-14 over 400 random pairs. Deliberately NOT labelled: 'binary-search-answer' (nothing monotone is being decided), 'segment-intersection' (a segment/segment hit test discriminates the closed-form cases but is absent from the ternary-search route, so it is route-specific scaffolding), 'shortest-path'/'dijkstra' (no graph), 'brute-force' (16 edge pairs is a constant). TRAPS FOUND AND FIXED WHILE SOLVING, both of which pass the single provided sample: (1) the outward apex image m + slant*n reproduces the sample to 1e-10 and is what the natural 'reflect the apex outward' reading gives, but it is the wrong unfolding - only the inward image m - slant*n makes the unfolded path cross the base edge, and with the outward one the closed form is wrong by up to 0.93 on random inputs (check (f)); the sanity check is h -> 0, where the inward image must land on the base centre. (2) An obstacle test on the ground leg is not merely unnecessary but harmful: rejecting edge pairs whose optimum tunnels through a base can discard a tied optimum, and the 1-Lipschitz exchange argument shows the unconstrained minimum already equals the answer. Verification: (a) the sample to 3e-10; (b) closed form vs nested ternary, 400 random pairs; (c) r(U) = sqrt(h^2+|c-U|^2) confirmed by Dijkstra on a fine triangulated mesh of one pyramid, res=30, to 6 decimals; (d) 60 random pairs against dense boundary sampling whose ground leg is a genuine visibility-graph shortest path around both square obstacles (no over-estimates, max gap 5.7e-5, i.e. sampling error); (e) the strongest check, a 3-D Dijkstra over a mesh of the entire surface - both pyramids plus ground, edges admitted only when the segment provably lies on the surface, so it assumes neither the one-face claim nor the straight-ground claim - bounding the answer from above within 0.0-0.4% on five configurations including two touching bases. Only one sample is published for this problem, so (c)-(e) rather than samples are what the confidence rests on. One residual uncertainty: the statement guarantees only that the bases intersect in zero area, so edge- and corner-touching bases are legal; these are handled (the ground leg degenerates to U = V) and one such case is in check (e), but no official test data was available to confirm.
